sources.title: Roy J. Glauber, The Quantum Theory of Optical Coherence, Physical Review 130, 2529–2539 (1963)
sources.locator: Complete 11-page APS PDF retrieved. Read §II, printed pp. 2530–2532, equations (2.14)–(2.18); §III, pp. 2532–2534, equations (3.1)–(3.14); and §IV, pp. 2534–2536, equations (4.8)–(4.10) and the coherent-field qualification.

contents.name: §II, equations (2.14)–(2.15): ideal point-detector absorption and the single-count rate
contents.support: Glauber models ideal absorption through a photon-annihilation matrix element and obtains a normally ordered E^(−)E^(+) rate by summing final states. The local postulate adopts the spectral law of a well-defined one-mode number PVM as an additional ideal detector assumption; it does not claim that the point-field rate derives this countable-outcome law.

source_review.read_extent: Read the full argument around equations (2.14)–(2.15), including the detector's frequency-independent absorption assumption and vacuum-counting discussion.
source_review.supports: The physical interpretation of absorption counting and normal ordering.
source_review.limitations: Glauber's detector is point-local and its field products are formal point-field expressions; the local item uses a normalized Hilbert-space mode and no point-field product.

contents.name: §II, equations (2.16)–(2.18): delayed coincidences and normally ordered higher counts
contents.support: The source derives the normally ordered two-count expression and extends it to n-fold delayed coincidences. The local theorem uses the same factorial ordering only after a finite-particle CCR identity and the one-mode count PVM are constructed.

source_review.read_extent: Read the complete two-detector and n-fold coincidence passage and its final-state sum.
source_review.supports: The relation between ideal coincidence counting and normally ordered field correlations.
source_review.limitations: The local theorem is a zero-delay same-mode result; it does not infer arbitrary separated-spacetime correlations from the point-field formulas.

contents.name: §III, equations (3.1)–(3.7): density-operator averages and first- and second-order field correlations
contents.support: The source defines density-operator averaging and G^(1), G^(2) for field components. The local postulate instead defines count probabilities by the count PVM and factorial moments by its scalar law, with the operator identity established locally.

source_review.read_extent: Read the density-operator convention and the full correlation definitions through equation (3.7).
source_review.supports: A source-backed photodetection and normally ordered correlation context.
source_review.limitations: The physical detector law remains adopted; this passage is not a proof of the local PVM's mathematical well-definedness.

contents.name: §III, equations (3.11)–(3.14): positivity inequalities for spacetime field correlations
contents.reason: These inequalities concern general spacetime field-correlation kernels, while this pair proves only a selected-mode factorial-moment identity and adds no correlation-kernel inequality.

contents.name: §IV, equations (4.8)–(4.10): factorization of coherent-field correlations
contents.support: Glauber describes field-eigenstate preparations whose correlation functions factorize. The local theorem defines a normalized coherent one-mode vector explicitly and proves its count law by shifting the exponential series; the field-factorization discussion is contextual only.

source_review.read_extent: Read the factorization definition and the positive-frequency field-eigenstate discussion through equations (4.8)–(4.10), including the paper's statement that detailed properties would be developed later.
source_review.supports: The coherent-state comparison in the normally ordered correlation discussion.
source_review.limitations: No point-field eigenstate theorem is imported; the state vector and its factorial moments are constructed and evaluated locally.

contents.name: §IV, nonstationary fields and the absence of a monochromaticity requirement for coherence
contents.support: The source distinguishes coherence from monochromaticity. The local postulate is formulated for a normalized transverse wavepacket and imposes no monochromatic-mode assumption.

source_review.read_extent: Read the full-text discussion of spectral bandwidth and nonstationary coherence in §IV.
source_review.supports: Wavepacket scope without a monochromaticity restriction.
source_review.limitations: No time-dependent correlation or detector bandwidth conclusion is claimed by the local postulate.

source_review.read_extent: Complete 11-page APS full text retrieved; assigned passages in §§II–IV were inspected in full.
source_review.supports: Historical and theoretical photodetection interpretation, normal ordering, and coherent-field correlation context.
source_review.limitations: The local mode PVM, its domains, and the state-distribution calculations are established by local mathematical proofs and explicit model postulates, not attributed to this paper.

sources.title: Daniel A. Steck, Quantum and Atom Optics, revision 0.16.10 (27 June 2026), complete author-hosted course text
sources.locator: Complete 1,198-page author-hosted PDF retrieved. Read Chapter 2 §§2.6.1–2.6.2, PDF pp. 74–76, and Chapter 16 §§16.1–16.4.2.4, PDF pp. 685–694.

recovery_attempts.outcome: The web reader rejected the complete 68,145,758-byte PDF as too large; a direct local download of the same author-hosted URL succeeded and the cited pages were inspected.

contents.name: Chapter 2 §2.6: the normalized second-order intensity correlation g^(2)(tau)
contents.support: The notes define normalized second-order intensity correlation. The local theorem defines its selected-mode zero-delay analogue directly through the number PVM's factorial moment and explicitly states the mode and moment hypotheses.

source_review.read_extent: Read the full derivation of the normalized second-order coherence definition and its classical constraints, PDF pp. 73–74.
source_review.supports: The normalized correlation convention and its interpretation as a second-order statistic.
source_review.limitations: The local item does not import the classical intensity inequality as a quantum count theorem.

contents.name: Chapter 2 §2.6.1: thermal light under the stationary complex-Gaussian field assumption
contents.support: The notes explicitly assume a stationary complex Gaussian random field and derive g^(2)(0)=2 from Gaussian moment factorization. The local theorem separately proves the same value for its explicitly defined quantum geometric occupation state; the classical Gaussian assumption is not imported into that proof.

source_review.read_extent: Read the complete thermal-light calculation and its Gaussian moment-factorization hypothesis, PDF pp. 74–75.
source_review.supports: The thermal second-order-correlation comparison and its value at zero delay.
source_review.limitations: The local theorem's state is a quantum diagonal density operator with geometric number probabilities, not a classical random field.

contents.name: Chapter 2 §2.6.2: Hanbury Brown–Twiss intensity-correlation apparatus
contents.reason: This section analyzes time-delayed experimental intensity correlations; the assigned pair contains no reported experiment, detector response model, or empirical HBT data.

contents.name: Chapter 16 §16.1, equations (16.3)–(16.12): single and joint photodetection probabilities with normal ordering
contents.support: The notes sum squared absorption amplitudes over final states to obtain E^(−)E^(+) and two-count E^(−)E^(−)E^(+)E^(+) expressions, explaining the vacuum-zero normal ordering. The local postulate gives a countable one-mode spectral-law assumption and proves the relation of its factorial operator on a precise Fock core.

source_review.read_extent: Read the full derivation from transition amplitudes through the first- and second-order detection expressions, PDF pp. 685–686.
source_review.supports: Normal-ordered photodetection interpretation and the single/two-count correlation structure.
source_review.limitations: The local postulate does not import a pointwise field product or claim this derivation proves countable PVM measurement for a detector.

contents.name: Chapter 16 §16.2, equations (16.13)–(16.18): unitary lossless beam-splitter mode transformation
contents.support: The source states the two-mode unitary transformation and the lossless condition |r|^2+|t|^2=1. The local theorem only uses this as model context; its explicit assumption is independent fixed-efficiency Bernoulli thinning.

source_review.read_extent: Read the full two-input/two-output transformation and unitarity constraints, PDF p. 687.
source_review.supports: An ideal optical loss-channel comparison for mode counts.
source_review.limitations: A lossless beam splitter is not itself a general nonideal detector; the local theorem states its independent constant-efficiency assumption explicitly.

contents.name: Chapter 16 §16.3, equations (16.19)–(16.24): one photon at a beam splitter and vanishing ideal joint count
contents.support: The source derives a one-photon output superposition and zero ideal two-output joint count. It also names accidental coincidences, finite detection times and dark counts as laboratory qualifications; the local example retains these as explicit exclusions.

source_review.read_extent: Read the complete single-photon beam-splitter argument and the paragraph on heralding, accidental coincidences, finite detection time and dark counts, PDF pp. 687–688.
source_review.supports: The conditional one-photon zero-factorial-correlation example and its apparatus limitations.
source_review.limitations: No reported experiment, measured probability or arbitrary multimode detector claim is inferred.

contents.name: Chapter 16 §16.4.1, equations (16.25)–(16.27): two photons in one input have a binomial beam-splitter count law
contents.support: For two photons in a single input, the notes obtain the binomial output probabilities and identify the single-photon transmission probability. The local theorem proves the factorial-moment scaling for arbitrary count laws under its stronger explicit independent-thinning model.

source_review.read_extent: Read the full same-input two-photon expansion and its stated binomial probabilities, PDF pp. 689–690.
source_review.supports: A finite-photon example of independent mode loss and the binomial count model.
source_review.limitations: The local theorem does not derive an arbitrary detector's efficiency channel from this lossless two-mode example.

contents.name: Chapter 16 §16.4.1, equations (16.28)–(16.31): two-input Hong–Ou–Mandel interference
contents.reason: This is a separate two-input interference result; the planned page proves one-mode count moments and independent loss, with no two-pulse or Hong–Ou–Mandel setup.

contents.name: Chapter 16 §16.4.2.1–16.4.2.2, equations (16.32)–(16.42): quasi-monochromatic beam and normalized pulse-mode creation
contents.support: The source defines a normalized pulse creation operator from a spectral envelope and obtains a normalized temporal envelope under a narrowband approximation. The local lemma constructs the exact abstract one-mode Fock splitting, number PVM and operator domains for any normalized Hilbert-space mode.

source_review.read_extent: Read the full continuum-mode and pulse-creation derivation, including the positive-frequency extension approximation, PDF pp. 690–692.
source_review.supports: The motivation for a normalized wavepacket mode and its one-mode Fock factorization.
source_review.limitations: The local mathematical result uses a general normalized Hilbert vector and does not assume narrow bandwidth or identify a time-local annihilation operator.

contents.name: Chapter 16 §16.4.2.3, equations (16.43)–(16.45): time-resolved annihilation operator and finite-window counts
contents.reason: The assigned postulate has a countable spectral mode measurement and makes no finite detection-window, time-resolved rate, or temporal response claim.

contents.name: Chapter 16 §16.4.2.4, equations (16.46)–(16.56): two-pulse overlap and delay-dependent coincidence curve
contents.reason: The delay-dependent two-pulse interference curve requires a beam splitter and two input modes, which are outside the specified single-mode correlation interfaces.

source_review.supports: A full independent textbook/lecture-note treatment of normal-ordered photodetection, coherent and thermal correlations, single-photon antibunching, beam-splitter loss and pulse-mode operators.
